Eight Adepts (also: Eight Adepts of Liyue, Bā Qí, Sanctification of Tao Dou): The Eight Adepts are a Liyue legend about eight gifted figures from the Archon War era who purified the tree-god Tao Dou, whose body stood before the realm of the dead. They were not all true adepti: three hermits of Guizang (Wind Reader, Yunlai Angler, Wuwang Kid), two sages of Lianshan (Sage Hu, Sage Jian), and three non-human Beasts of Tao Dou (Lone Butterfly of the Crimson Flame, Jade-Plumed Silverwing, Gold-Eyed Celadon Mare). One of them gave her life to make the working succeed. The story was introduced during the 5.3 Lantern Rite event, a limited-time event.

Keqing describes them as legendary people said to have had adeptus-like abilities, which earned the name rather than any formal rank. The tale is told by storytellers (the opera "The Sanctification of Tao Dou" is performed at the Lantern Rite), passed on through clan genealogies such as the Lan clan's, and kept alive in practice by the Wangsheng Funeral Parlor.

In 6.3 the Lantern Rite story A Lanternlit Ode to the Silver Moon connected the Celadon Mare to Zibai, who is now a living figure in Liyue, so part of the legend is also anchored in present-day events.

Practice: The legend runs as follows. During the Archon War a giant tree-god, Tao Dou, stood on a divine mountain, and Liyue believed the realm of the dead lay behind it; those who committed grave sins could not pass beyond. Dragged into the fighting, the god disturbed the realm and the line between life and death blurred. The Eight rose to deal with it and laid down a great array, the Seven-and-Eight-Gates Method, which uses eight nodes of Liyue's ley lines with a person at each. One gate is chosen to be obfuscated, erasing whoever guards it from the ley lines to seal the gate and keep evil from escaping. The Lone Butterfly of the Crimson Flame held that gate and vanished from the world. Afterwards Tao Dou's remains sank into the ley lines and became the border between the living and the dead.

The members, as the legend names them:
- Three Hermits of Guizang: Wind Reader (Mad Lan), founder of the Qimen arts, from the Twelve Tribes of Chenyu Vale; the Yunlai Angler (Fish Creel), whose rod technique is the root of Yunlai Swordsmanship; and Wuwang Kid (Old Man Wuwang, Red Runt), always presented as a child, expert in Qihuang sigils to catch demons, heal illness and protect life from death.
- Two Sages of Lianshan: Sage Hu (gourd crafts) and Sage Jian (bronze mirrors). Little survives about them beyond their secret Lianshan art and a hidden palace, traditionally believed to lie in the mountains south of Stone Gate, where they cultivated.
- Three Beasts of Tao Dou, also called the Three Immortals: the Lone Butterfly of the Crimson Flame (Art of Homa), the Jade-Plumed Silverwing (a swallow) and the Gold-Eyed Celadon Mare (a white horse), all auspicious beasts able to take human form.

After the working, legend says Silverwing and Wind Reader went wandering together while the white horse retreated into seclusion in the mountains. Wuwang Kid, who admired the Lone Butterfly, took up her mantle and taught her methods to the founders of the Wangsheng Funeral Parlor.

Zibai's voice-over lines, as the wiki summarises them, say Wind Reader and Silverwing met once each autumn after the Tao Dou affair, and that the Eight came together because they frequented the same tea shop. Some used nicknames among themselves: Mad Lan, White Foal (the Celadon Mare), Red Runt, Fish Creel. Wind Reader and Wuwang Kid are also described as swordsmen. These details come from the wiki's summary of Zibai's profile material and were not traced to the lines themselves.

Regional variation: The legend belongs to Liyue. Different places keep different threads: Chenyu Vale's Lan clan claims descent from Wind Reader's brothers and keeps the Qimen arts and a silver sparrow as a family symbol; the Wangsheng Funeral Parlor carries Wuwang Kid's and the Lone Butterfly's tradition; Yunlai Swordsmanship (the style Keqing trains in) descends from the Angler. Ordinary Liyue folk know it mainly as a story told in opera and by storytellers.

The three Hidden Palaces named after ancient divination texts (Guizang, Lianshan and Zhou) echo the legend's groups: the Zhou palace is the one a book says was enchanted with the Seven-and-Eight-Gates method to suppress evils, the most revered being Tao Dou.

Scene use: Use it as shared folk history, retold with flourishes and some doubt. Liyue residents tell it around the Lantern Rite, characters tied to the Lan clan or the funeral parlour take quiet pride in it, and Keqing will correct embellishments. Do not present members as certainly dead or alive: it is a legend with a few confirmed anchors.

Characters who know more (Zhongli, Zibai) speak with the ease of eyewitnesses and do not need to prove the story. Characters without that knowledge should treat the Eight as figures from a storyteller's tale, and should not give every member the same abilities.

Examples: - In the 5.3 quest, Lan Yan's rattan figures, eight movable dolls modelled on the legend, prompt Keqing to explain the Eight, and Yun Jin later retells the Lone Butterfly's sacrifice before her performance of the Tao Dou opera.
- In the same event the Seven-and-Eight-Gates Method is revived by Ningguang, Hu Tao and the Ministry of Civil Affairs: Hu Tao is chosen to be obfuscated at the Gate of Death, and other gates are watched by Keqing, Qiqi with Baizhu, Ganyu, Ningguang with Lan Yan, Xiao, Beidou with the Crux, and Yelan. Lan Yan's rattan dolls of Hu Tao link the overseers to share the burden of fetor.

Lan Yan's silver hairpiece is modelled on Silverwing; Hu Tao recognises it as the Jade-Plumed Silverwing, one of the Three Immortals of Tao Dou.

1.content:
A secret Liyue art that suppresses evil spirits, even gods. It places a person at each of eight key nodes of Liyue's ley lines (the gates) and obfuscates one, erasing its guardian from the lines to seal evil in. The seven in its name is the number of gates left once it is working. The gates and their latest positions, per the wiki: Life at Yilong Wharf, Death at Wuwang Hill, Repose at Qingce Village, Concealment at Mt. Aocang, Initiation at Liyue Harbor, Terrain at Dihua Marsh, Fright at Guyun Stone Forest and Injury at the Chasm. The nodes move as human activity changes the ley lines. A Descender, who is not recorded on the ley lines, would not vanish if obfuscated. The knowledge was lost over time and no record remains in Yuehai Pavilion; the 5.3 event revives it with help from an anonymous letter from the adepti.

The gate names derive from the Chinese divination Qimen Dunjia. Of the eight, Life, Repose and Initiation are auspicious, Death, Fright and Injury inauspicious, and Concealment and Terrain neutral.

key: Lone Butterfly of the Crimson Flame
2.comment: Eight Adepts: Lone Butterfly of the Crimson Flame
2.content: One of the Three Beasts of Tao Dou, an adeptus of the Art of Homa. In the legend she was in charge of the gate that was chosen to be obfuscated, so she disappeared from the world; she was the only one of the eight to sacrifice herself. Wuwang Kid admired her, took up her mantle and passed the work of guarding the line between life and death to the founders of the Wangsheng Funeral Parlor.

3.content: One of the Three Hermits of Guizang, said to have always presented himself in child form. His speciality was Qihuang sigils for catching demons, healing illness and protecting lives from death. The Wangsheng Funeral Parlor's founders are said to have studied under him, and he took up the Lone Butterfly's legacy. The wiki presumes him dead; canon does not say so.

4.content: One of the Three Hermits of Guizang and the founder of the Qimen arts, said to come from the Twelve Tribes of Chenyu Vale. The Lan clan, including Lan Yan, claims descent from his two brothers. After Tao Dou he travelled with Silverwing. Zibai recalls that he never sought longevity and must long since have died.

5.content: One of the Three Beasts of Tao Dou, a swallow and, per the wiki, the one member who is truly an adeptus. Lan Yan's silver hairpiece is a family heirloom modelled after her, and the Lan clan treats her as a symbol. Zhongli compares her to the Ship of Theseus: as long as swallows fly in Liyue she remains, though her memories are replaced as swallows come and go.

6.content: A white horse, one of the Three Beasts of Tao Dou, identified by the 6.3 Lantern Rite story with Zibai's Third Deadly Self Ziqiao, whom Zhongli (Morax) freed from the Zhanzhu painting during the Archon War. After Tao Dou her powers waned and she retreated into the Qingce mountains. In the 6.3 event she was restored as Zibai and now stays at Baiju Guesthouse by arrangement with the Wangsheng Funeral Parlor. Her own entry carries the details.

Exorcists and Thaumaturges (also: Exorcist, Exorcists, Thaumaturge, Thaumaturges, Liyue exorcism, Tianheng Thaumaturges, Lan Clan): Exorcists, also called thaumaturges, are Liyue practitioners who have sworn to cleanse the land of ghosts, spirits and demons. They combine spells and talismans with martial arts, and most come from families that pass the trade down. Chongyun, heir of the Tianheng Thaumaturges, is the best-known; Shenhe, born into a branch of the same clan but trained by an adeptus, is called by him an adept exorcist.

Canon names only a few groups: the Tianheng Thaumaturges (Chongyun's clan), the family of Yelan, and the Lan clan of Chenyu Vale. Exorcists are mortals, distinct from the adepti, though their techniques resemble adepti arts and some exorcists have had adepti friends.

Practice: Exorcism is learned inside families and treated as a duty to protect Liyue. Methods mix mantras, talismans and sword work; Chongyun holds that thaumaturgy plus martial arts is the true way.

Clans keep records. The Tianheng Thaumaturges hold generational books of the evil spirits they have defeated, and Chongyun's illustrations in them are imprecise because he has never met a spirit. A mantra attributed to the clan runs "Heart be pure, evil be erased. Mind be purged, world be saved", which Chongyun admits he tends to forget the end of. Timing and weather matter to him: he treats noon as the peak of spiritual energy and rain as the purest water, and he trusts thunder to make evil cower.

Tools are individual. Chongyun fights with an ice-made spirit blade; Shenhe's mother carried an exorcism dagger that Shenhe later inherited. Exorcists also perform prayer rituals: on Chongyun's birthday he prays with clan elders on Mt. Tianheng.

Work is commission-based and often anticlimactic. Rumours of hauntings frequently turn out false, and Chongyun usually charges only a small fee. Haunted houses are typical jobs (in one tale he cleared a wealthy woman's home in Liyue Harbor simply by sitting in it).

The craft overlaps with Liyue's other mystic traditions. Adeptus arts include talismans (sigils) that store adeptal power, and Qimen arts, practised by the Lan clan, cover fortune-telling, illusion-making and warding off evil. The Fantastic Compass shows another overlap: made by the adeptus Sea Gazer to seal monsters, it was given to a mortal thaumaturge friend, and the two later used it together against great demons in the mountains.

Whether exorcism needs a Vision is open. Everyone seen casting in play has one, yet Yelan says her family has practised magic for generations and built catalysts only they can use, which implies the art is not limited to Vision-bearers.

Limits and failure modes recur in character material: Chongyun's pure yang constitution (a "congenital positivity" in the official introduction) repels evil so strongly that he has performed hundreds of exorcisms without ever seeing a ghost. He regards this as an unearned crutch and trains in orthodox technique to prove himself. This is an individual quirk, not a general trait of exorcists.

Regional variation: Exorcism is a Liyue profession. Other nations have their own supernatural arts under other names; none is called exorcism in canon.

Within Liyue, practice differs by clan. The Tianheng Thaumaturges (Mt. Tianheng) are shown through Chongyun with mantras, talismans, an ice-made spirit blade and generational records of defeated spirits. The Lan clan of Chenyu Vale, descended from the brothers of Lan Junming (the Wind Reader among the Eight Adepts), practise Qimen arts, using them for duty or hobby crafts, and serve as consultants to the Moonchase Festival at Yilong Wharf.

In Inazuma, onmyoudou was created 500 years ago by Kamuna Harunosuke, who combined Liyue adepti techniques with an art he learned from the Yougou Tengu. Yae Miko's yakan kitsune spirits are implied to be shikigami of that tradition. This is related to, but not described in canon as, exorcism.

Scene use: Use exorcists as polite local specialists called in for hauntings, who often find the problem smaller than the rumour.

A scene might feature a hired exorcist reading the room for yin and yang imbalance, setting talismans, and chanting a mantra before facing a haunting. Keep results grounded: many cases are mundane or fraudulent, and Liyue folk may respect exorcists while also doubting them. Chongyun admires Xiao as Conqueror of Demons but resents Xiao's remarks that exorcists' repertoire is lacking and their power trivial.

Tone guidance: exorcists take their oath seriously, hold family tradition dear, and speak in measured, courteous terms. A lineage story (a clan reunion, a missing relative, a catalyst heirloom) fits better than a free-standing monster hunt.

Examples: Chongyun, who sits motionless in a dark corner until spirits flee, is the standard example.

- Chongyun: heir of the Tianheng Thaumaturges; a pure yang spirit makes spirits flee, but he wants to earn the title by technique.
- Shenhe: from a Tianheng branch family, never taught exorcism by her parents, later the disciple of Cloud Retainer; her adepti techniques resemble exorcist ones.
- Yelan: descendant of the exorcist brothers Boyang and Rongzhao; she is not known to practise the family trade.
- Lan Yan and Lan Ying: Lan clan members who make rattan Warding Figures with built-in Qimen mechanisms.

Status as of 7.1: As of 7.1 exorcists remain active in Liyue. The Lan clan featured in the Silverwing in Pursuit of the Moon event (7.1, limited-time). No exorcist-related content in Nod-Krai or Snezhnaya content (6.x to 7.1) was found.

8.content:
The Tianheng Thaumaturges are an exorcist clan of Liyue with many exorcists in its ranks, associated with Mt. Tianheng. Chongyun is a clan heir; Shenhe, his aunt, came from a branch family. The clan elders were delighted to learn that Shenhe was alive and prepared gifts and an auspicious day for a reunion, though she is hard to find. Yuandai, a crane disciple of Cloud Retainer who lived as a human, is recorded as having fallen in love with an exorcist from Mt. Tianheng and had a son; her granddaughter is Shuyu. The clan keeps generational records of the spirits it has defeated.

Shenhe's parents belong to the clan's recent history. Her mother died when Shenhe was small, and her father, maddened, tried to sacrifice her to an evil being when she was about six, so Shenhe was never trained by the clan.

9.comment: Exorcists and Thaumaturges: Yelan's Ancestors and the Fantastic Compass
9.content: The Fantastic Compass was made by the adeptus Sea Gazer to seal monsters, and then passed to a mortal thaumaturge friend. Roughly 500 years ago, Yelan's ancestors Boyang and Rongzhao, both exorcists, brought it to the battle at the Chasm against the Abyss alongside the Yaksha Bosacius. Boyang and other Millelith lured monsters into a space that could suppress the Abyss and sealed them in with the compass, while Rongzhao helped from outside (the Fantastic Compass page credits Boyang and Bosacius with the seal). Rongzhao returned alone and driven mad by Bosacius' karma. Yelan's clan survived and developed catalysts only they can operate.

10.comment: Exorcists and Thaumaturges: Lan Clan and Qimen Arts
10.content: The Lan clan of Chenyu Vale descends from the brothers of Lan Junming, the Wind Reader of the Eight Adepts, who taught them Qimen arts after returning from wandering. He encouraged pursuing the arts both as hobby and duty and also taught a Soul-Binding Art that was later outlawed as violating the natural order. Over centuries the clan became integral to Chenyu Vale's commissions and the Moonchase Festival. Some members make silver ornaments of the Jade-Plumed Silverwing. Lan Yu is the current head; Lan Yan, Lan Ying, Aunt Lan and Uncle Lan are other known members.

11.comment: Exorcists and Thaumaturges: Lan Ying and the Warding Figures
11.content: During the Silverwing in Pursuit of the Moon event (limited-time, 7.1), Lan Ying, Lan Yan's second cousin, explained that clan thaumaturges are too busy with large spirits to clear the small clumps of evil energy that can sicken ordinary people. With Lan Yan she devised rattan Warding Figures containing a Qimen core that absorbs and seals such energy.

12.comment: Exorcists and Thaumaturges: Chongyun's Exorcism Creed
12.content: Chongyun considers exorcists protectors of Liyue since ancient times, with techniques handed down from generation to generation. He opposes using his inborn yang energy as a substitute for technique, and in his Hangout Event he follows rumours that mostly prove baseless. He thinks Xiao is disparaging toward exorcists and finds the Wangsheng Funeral Parlor's easy smile irritating, though he praises the parlor's integrity and respects Xiao as the Conqueror of Demons.

13.content:
Lantern Rite Festival (also: Lantern Rite, Lantern Rite Gala, Mingxiao Lantern, Xiao Lantern, Xiao Lanterns, Xiao Market): Lantern Rite is Liyue's biggest festival of the year, held over five days around the first full moon of the year and celebrated across the nation, above all in Liyue Harbor. People pray for peace, ward off evil, eat seasonal food and release Xiao Lanterns carrying written wishes into the night sky. On the final night the city releases the Mingxiao Lantern, a huge floating lantern built from donated materials and shaped after a fallen hero, usually an adeptus who died protecting Liyue. According to Zhongli, the custom began in a war long ago as lanterns lit to guide soldiers home; after the Archon War it became a festival of remembrance.

For the yaksha Xiao the festival is anything but restful: the lingering hatred of gods Morax defeated erupts most violently during Lantern Rite, so he spends the festival fighting unseen outside the city.

Practice: - **Xiao Lanterns**: small floating lanterns made from a wrapping of lantern fiber, a wick and a shard of Plaustrite, the Liyue mineral that floats once activated. People write wishes on wish sticks, insert them and release the lantern.
- **Mingxiao Lantern**: the festival's centerpiece, a giant lantern built by the whole city and released on the last night.
- **Feasting and gatherings**: families and friends meet over a holiday meal and see out the old year together.

- **Mingxiao Lantern details** (per the 1.3 festival planner Jiangzhou): everyone who can gives materials or money, and much of the funding comes from market vendors. Its size depends on the largest piece of Plaustrite unearthed in the preceding year, which sits at the lantern's core. Its design honors the adeptus form of a hero who died for Liyue, and Yuehai Pavilion chooses the subject partly by popular demand.
- **Xiao Market**: the festival market of stalls and vendors in Liyue Harbor; Jiangzhou, a planner at the Lantern Rite Gala, lists it among the festival's main traditions alongside the two kinds of lantern.
- **Organisation**: the festival has several planners, because the whole of Liyue Harbor turns out (Jiangzhou was one in 1.3); the Ministry of Civil Affairs handles lantern clean-up, and in later years the Qixing set each festival's theme.
- **Clean-up**: Xiao Lanterns do not simply vanish. Badly made ones break up in the air and leave loose, flying Plaustrite; others snag in trees and corners. The Ministry of Civil Affairs assigns someone, in 1.3 the Millelith soldier Hongyu, to gather fallen lanterns as the festival goes on.

- **Prayers to the adepti**: during festival seasons Liyue people burn incense and pray to the adepti of Jueyun Karst for protection. Xiao's profile notes that nobody prays to him, since a demon-slaying yaksha brings no luck or fortune. Hu Tao (6.3) observes that at Lantern Rite adepti and ancestors are venerated alike, and goes to pay respects to her ancestors.
- **Exorcism roots**: Xiao's profile says many human festivals mark days when the adepti defeated man-eating monsters; people imitated those deeds in exorcism rituals that grew into celebrations. The festival's prayers to "ward off evil" echo this.
- **Seasonal food**: in 6.3 Xiangling names Triple-Layered Consommé and "Come and Get It" as Wanmin Restaurant's Lantern Rite specialties.
- **Recent additions**: each year the Qixing add a theme. Fireworks were added in 2.4 and kites (mixing Liyue kite craft with Fontaine's Mechanical Vertical Lifting Device) in 4.4. In 3.4 a concert of the Fontaine musician Dvorak's Iridescence Tour was held, and in 5.3 Yun Jin staged the opera "The Sanctification of Tao Dou".

History: Zhongli says that in an ancient war the people of Liyue released lanterns to remind their soldiers of the way home and to never lose sight of themselves, and that few people today remember this. After the Archon War the custom became a way to commemorate those who gave their lives, and grew into a full festival of remembrance and unity.

Jiangzhou explains the belief that the fire's light "keeps wisdom alive" and guides fallen heroes home along the sea, so they can be reunited with the living. The communal Mingxiao Lantern has been built since peace was restored, to keep alive the spirit of unity.

Xiao's character story ties the festival to the gods Morax defeated: their hatred and leftover power, half-awake and half-dreaming, sometimes erupt with abnormal force, and the eruption during Lantern Rite is the largest. Xiao must perform the "Nuo Dance of Evil Conquering" and fights day and night through the festival, so he has come to hate it, though he feels something he cannot name (loneliness, peace or fear for the future) when the lantern-light shines over the sea.

Regional variation: Liyue Harbor is the heart of the festival: the Lantern Rite Gala, decorated streets and stalls up Feiyun Slope, the Mingxiao Lantern at the harbor and fireworks or kites over the water. Smaller celebrations happen elsewhere: Qingce Village takes part (one 1.3 request is titled "Qingce's Lanterns"), and in 1.3 the staff of Wangshu Inn brought the festival to the inn for Xiao. The adepti mark it in their own way: in 2.4 Keqing delivered festive gifts to Cloud Retainer, Madame Ping and Xiao, and the adepti appear watching the fireworks.

Visitors join in. Mondstadters visiting Liyue appear in the 1.3 festival requests, and foreign guests feature in later years: Dvorak of Fontaine in 3.4, Charlotte, Navia, Clorinde, Furina and Neuvillette around 4.4. In 6.3 Yanfei compares Liyue's moon legends with records she found among Nod-Krai's Frostmoon Scions.

Scene use: Use Lantern Rite for a warm, crowded, festive Liyue scene: lantern-lit streets, crowded stalls, the smell of festival dishes, people writing wishes on wish sticks, and the moment when the whole harbor looks up as the Mingxiao Lantern rises. It suits reunions, confessions of wishes, family meals and seeing out the old year. A quieter angle is grief and remembrance: the lanterns were meant to guide the dead home.

Practical notes for roleplay:
- Typical greeting: "Happy Lantern Rite!"
- Liyue characters treat it as the year's big holiday; officials (the Qixing, the Ministry of Civil Affairs, the Millelith) are swamped with work.
- Xiao avoids crowds and is usually absent, fighting outside the city; drawing him into the festival is a recurring kindness his friends attempt, and he watches from a distance at most.
- The adepti are honored, but the festival is run by humans; Keqing notes in 4.4 that with Liyue now ruled by people, the Qixing update the festival to keep up with the times.
- Don't invent a specific Mingxiao Lantern subject for a year canon has not named.

Examples: Lantern Rites the Traveler has attended (each was a limited-time event; dates are release versions):
- **1.3**: the Mingxiao Lantern honored Skybracer. A would-be thief's absurd plan to steal its Plaustrite was foiled, and the Wangshu Inn staff brought the festival to Xiao, who watched the lantern rise from outside the city.
- **2.4**: fireworks joined the festival under Ningguang and Keqing; Keqing, overworked, was coaxed into resting and watching the fireworks.
- **3.4**: the Mingxiao Lantern was modeled on Sea Gazer; a Lantern Rite concert was held with Dvorak.
- **4.4**: a kite theme; the Mingxiao Lantern depicted the yaksha Menogias.
- **5.3**: the festival coincided with a crisis of fetor (death energy) around Wuwang Hill.
- **6.3**: the Mingxiao Lantern honored the White Horse Adeptus.

- **1.3 details**: the 1.3 Lantern's Plaustrite was the largest found in twenty years. Skybracer, by legend, had his antlers cut off to prop up the collapsing Mt. Tianheng and kept fighting until he died. The Lantern Rite Tales requests that year included Hongyu's lantern clean-up.
- **2.4 details**: Ningguang had fireworks added after the year's upheavals; stolen firework shipments to Qingce Village were traced to Treasure Hoarders. The festival also followed Ningguang's rebuilding of the Jade Chamber.
- **3.4 details**: Dvorak came looking for the adeptus who had once saved his ancestor, who turned out to be Madame Ping. Hu Tao's opening act with Yun Jin and Xinyan preceded the concert, and the year closed with a get-together at Xinyue Kiosk that drew Zhongli, Xiao and Venti.
- **4.4 details**: Xianyun used her adeptal power to send up her own kite, catching the released kites in its wake and lifting them all higher, and Gaming's wushou performance won over his father.
- **5.3 details**: Hu Tao led the "Sanctification of Tao Dou" ritual, with Xiao, Baizhu, Qiqi, Ningguang and Lan Yan covering the other Qimen gates while she took the Gate of Death; the Traveler pulled her back from the border of death. Yun Jin then performed an opera of the same name at Yilong Wharf.

Status as of 7.1: As of Version 7.1, Lantern Rite remains an annual, living Liyue tradition. The most recent one shown in canon is the 6.3 festival (in-game event January-February 2026); the 7.0-7.1 Snezhnaya content contains no Lantern Rite.

14.content: The Mingxiao Lantern is the giant communal lantern at the center of Liyue's Lantern Rite, released over Liyue Harbor on the festival's final night. Citizens and visitors donate materials and money, vendors at the market cover much of the cost, and its size depends on the largest Plaustrite found in the previous year. Its design is normally the adeptus form of a hero who died protecting Liyue, picked by Yuehai Pavilion with public input. Subjects in canon: Skybracer (1.3), Sea Gazer (3.4), the yaksha Menogias (4.4), reportedly the god Tao Dou (5.3), and the White Horse Adeptus (6.3, a horse-shaped lantern).

15.content: Xiao Lanterns are the small personal floating lanterns of Lantern Rite. Their "Xiao" means sky (霄), not the adeptus Xiao (魈), though the two are pronounced alike. Each is made from lantern-fiber wrapping, a wick and a Plaustrite shard to lift it. People write wishes on wish sticks, slot them in and let the lantern carry the wish into the night. Item text: "It floats away carrying beautiful wishes." Children learn to make them (Yaoyao teaches Qiqi in 6.3), and stalls in Liyue Harbor help visitors craft their own. The Ministry of Civil Affairs has stray and broken ones collected because loose Plaustrite is a hazard.

16.comment: Lantern Rite Festival: Xiao and Lantern Rite
16.content: For Xiao, Lantern Rite means the worst of his duty. The resentment of the gods Morax defeated erupts most strongly during the festival, and he performs the "Nuo Dance of Evil Conquering" day and night to keep Liyue safe, so he has come to hate the festival. He avoids the crowds. His friends keep trying to share it with him: in 1.3 Verr Goldet, Huai'an and the Traveler held a festival at Wangshu Inn and led him close enough to see the Mingxiao Lantern rise. In later years he gradually joins small gatherings, like the 3.4 dinner at Xinyue Kiosk, which made him visibly nervous.

17.comment: Lantern Rite Festival: White Horse Adeptus lantern (6.3)
17.content: At the Lantern Rite of Version 6.3 ("Luna IV", story quest "A Lanternlit Ode to the Silver Moon"), the Mingxiao Lantern honored the White Horse Adeptus. Liyue legend says she lives in a palace on the moon, descends to grant people's wishes, and once aided Rex Lapis in the Archon War. Xingqiu links this to why wishes are written on Xiao Lanterns. The adeptus, Zibai, turned out to be real: Zhongli revealed that she had long since died, but one of the Three Deadly Selves she severed was trapped in the shadowmoon, and he estimated that the many wishes released on Xiao Lanterns on the festival night would trigger the shadowmoon's collapse. Another of her selves, Ziqiao, whom Paimon passed off as someone "cosplaying" the adeptus, laughed at the lantern's inaccurate horse gait and was moved that her story had not been forgotten. Ziqiao also remarked on how Xiao Lanterns resemble the Moon Lanterns once offered to the heavens; Zhongli insists they are different, and the link is unconfirmed. The story quest stayed permanently available after the event.

18.content:
Contracts in Liyue (also: Liyue contracts, Sanctity of contracts, Wrath of the Rock, Contract to End All Contracts): Contracts are the heart of Liyue. Its god, Morax (Rex Lapis, now Zhongli), is the God of Contracts, and the nation treats agreements as binding in everything from a merchant's invoice to the ancient laws he laid down. Those laws are policed by the Liyue Qixing. The god's own warning is that whoever breaks their word will suffer the Wrath of the Rock. Fairness is the point: in Zhongli's words, a contract that has lost fairness is only proof of deception.

The idea reaches beyond commerce. Morax made contracts with the adepti to defend Liyue Harbor, with the dragon Azhdaha to spare humanity, and finally with the Tsaritsa, the "contract to end all contracts" by which he gave up his Gnosis. Ordinary people live under the same logic through trade rules, the Qixing's law book and the habit of settling matters in explicit terms.

Contracts in Liyue are both law and moral idea. The legal side is a very old rulebook that every Tianquan amends. The moral side is reciprocity, "equivalent exchange": a contract binds both parties, and exploiting its letter against its spirit fails the principle.

Practice: Merchants live by deadlines, invoices and shipping destinations. Harbor trade runs under what the in-game description of Liyue Harbor calls countless contracts and regulations. The Qixing punish violators.

Morax's ancient laws touch every part of city life, from simple monetary exchange and agreements between merchants to the framework of the city itself. Outlanders, as Linlang remarks to Paimon, like to say that Mondstadt is to freedom as Liyue is to contracts.

Zhongli says the God of Contracts remembers the name of every person he meets and the sailing date of every ship, because holding so many contracts requires it, and adds that not every memory is a happy one (voice-over about the God of Contracts).

Fairness is the test of a good contract. Zhongli says that asking people to follow a contract is only asking them to respect fairness, and that when fairness is lost the contract becomes proof of one's deception. He also says contracts cannot define friendship or measure sentiment, and that a Vision is itself a kind of contract: power comes with responsibility.

The law book is a living document. Each generation of Qixing interprets the old laws and adds subtle amendments to close loopholes. Merchants treat undiscovered loopholes as "permissible if unaddressed" and exploit them until the Qixing patch them. Zhongli's Character Story says the amendment book had reached 279 pages, and that Ningguang, the Tianquan who maintains it, is jokingly nicknamed the "Tailor of Liyue" for patching so quickly. The Qixing divide the work: the Tianquan keeps the law book and foreign relations, and per Keqing's voice-over the Yuheng's post is subject to over a hundred contractual obligations.

Beyond the state, small agreements govern daily trade, such as hired escorts. Independent Local Security Agencies guard goods on the roads, and the wiki notes that because they are privately run the Qixing have struggled to standardise them. At the Rite of Descension the local Linlang tells the Traveler that the Qixing are mere mortals while Rex Lapis is forever with Liyue, a sign that ordinary people still ground the whole system in the god's promise.

Regional variation: Outside Liyue, the nation is known for this ideal: Paimon tells the Traveler that Mondstadt is to freedom as Liyue is to contracts. People from all seven nations come to trade at Liyue Harbor, and in practice foreign merchants work under Liyue's rules there.

Zhongli's voice-over on Furina respects that she made a contract with herself and held to it for over five centuries, a case from another nation that he judges by the same standard: justice that makes exacting demands on oneself, not only on others.

Scene use: Use contracts as the natural way for Liyue characters to settle trust: terms are stated, and a breach has a stated price. Merchants and officials can quote clauses, deadlines and amendments. Zhongli especially frames companionship and favours as a contract with fair terms (in his voice-overs he asks what name to sign under and notes who pays travel expenses). Do not make everyone legalistic; the depth of the principle shows mainly in how seriously a promise is taken once given.

Good scene hooks: a loophole being exploited and the Qixing patching it; a merchant who has missed a deadline; an adept or old servant who still honours an ancient agreement; a foreigner who treats words lightly. Fairness is what to dramatise: a one-sided clause is shameful, not clever. Treat the Wrath of the Rock as a moral warning rather than an everyday mechanic.

Examples: - Morax and the adepti: at the founding of Liyue Harbor he contracted the adepti to defend it.
- Morax and Azhdaha: the Geo dragon agreed not to harm humanity or Liyue, and to be sealed underground again if he did.
- Morax and the Tsaritsa: he handed over his Gnosis under the "contract to end all contracts" (revealed in A New Star Approaches).

- Ganyu serves the Qixing as secretary in honour of her contract with Rex Lapis; its dating is disputed (see uncertainties).
- Xiao is one of the adepti the wiki lists among those who signed a contract with Morax to defend Liyue, and he is the one most actively hunting demons.
- Sal Flore: Zhongli set a contract for two treasure-seekers in Havria's ruins, to take turns claiming finds. Both broke it in turn and he dealt with each.
- Azhdaha's erosion: over time the dragon forgot Morax's face and the contract, then turned on the people he had sworn to spare, a case of a contract failing through memory loss rather than malice.

19.comment: Contracts in Liyue: Wrath of the Rock
19.content:
The saying attributed to Rex Lapis is that the one who reneges on their words shall suffer the Wrath of the Rock. Zhongli's Character Story quotes it as the one law standing above all mortal amendments, and it is the sanction behind Liyue's contract culture.

In the Chinese text the line is also a pun, since the word for breaking one's word (shiyan) sounds like the word for being swallowed by rock, according to the wiki's translation notes. The sources do not describe a mechanical curse; treat it as moral and legal authority.

20.comment: Contracts in Liyue: Contract to End All Contracts
20.content:
In A New Star Approaches, Zhongli reveals that he staged his own apparent death at the Rite of Descension to test whether Liyue could do without him, and that he had contracted with the Tsaritsa to give up his Gnosis. Signora collected it. He calls it the contract to end all contracts.

His Character Story 5 notes that losing his divine ability to defend Liyue is a heavy price, and that in an equivalent exchange the Cryo Archon must have wagered something to balance the scales. What she gave is not spelled out in the sources checked (see uncertainties).

21.comment: Contracts in Liyue: The Book of Liyue's Laws
21.content:
The Tianquan keeps the collected ancient laws of Morax and every amendment. Zhongli's Character Story gives the book as 279 pages and calls Ningguang the "Tailor of Liyue" for patching loopholes quickly.

The Qixing as a whole interpret the law and punish violators, and other members help draft laws. For example, livelihood matters like water supply are the Yuheng's job, yet the Urban Areas Sanitation Act, against sabotage of water sources, was amended by the Tianquan.

22.content:
Morax brought Azhdaha up from Nantianmen and gave him sight; the dragon agreed never to harm humanity or Liyue and to be sealed underground again if he did. Erosion later made him forget Morax and the contract.

Azhdaha's later attacks forced Morax and the adepti to intervene and seal him. The sources frame this as the cost of a contract with an eroding being.

23.content:
At the founding of Liyue Harbor, Morax contracted the adepti to defend it while he continued fighting. Ganyu, Xiao, Madame Ping, Cloud Retainer, Moon Carver, Mountain Shaper and Yanfei's father are the adepti the wiki lists as still defending Liyue.

Zhongli credits Liyue's prosperity not only to Rex Lapis but to the servants who honoured their end of the contract, and says Ganyu has served the longest. Accounts of when each contract began disagree (see uncertainties).

24.content:
Liyue Cuisine (also: Liyue food, Liyue dishes, Li-style and Yue-style cooking): Liyue cuisine is the food culture of the Geo nation of contracts, built around two long-rival styles. Li style is bold and rich, using ingredients from the mountains; Yue style is lighter and seafood-based. In Liyue Harbor the best-regarded houses of each are Liuli Pavilion (Li) and Xinyue Kiosk (Yue), both on Feiyun Slope. At Chihu Rock, the humbler side of the city, Wanmin Restaurant, run by Chef Mao with his daughter Xiangling as head chef, ignores the quarrel and cooks inventive, spicy, everyday food. Tea is very popular, with Qiaoying Village famous for its leaves.

Food is a point of pride and of argument in Liyue: fans of one style clash with fans of the other, and the two rival restaurants need booking months ahead (Xinyue Kiosk is noted as expensive). Locals value good ingredients, spice and presentation; the Liyue gourmet Xi'er judges Liyue's seasoning and presentation a cut above Mondstadt's.

Practice: Liyue has two main culinary styles, as the gourmet Xi'er explains. Li style favours bold, rich, indulgent flavours and draws on mountain ingredients. Yue style favours lighter, brighter flavours and leans heavily on seafood. The two have a long history and a bitter, equally long rivalry. In Liyue Harbor's shopping district, Feiyun Slope, Liuli Pavilion is the leading Li-style house and Xinyue Kiosk the most authentic Yue-style one; Xinyue Kiosk's menu is mentioned as including Crystal Shrimp, Golden Crab and Fullmoon Egg. Xinyue Kiosk is noted as expensive; both need booking months ahead. Chihu Rock, the poorer side of the city, leans towards street food, with up-and-coming restaurants such as Wanmin Restaurant. Dishes in item text include Zhongyuan Chop Suey (a strong-flavoured comfort dish, described as the authentic "Liyue taste" for older folk), Jueyun Guoba (a crisp rice-and-horsetail crust topped with ham and Jueyun Chili, the snack Xiangling's companion Guoba is named after), Almond Tofu (a chilled almond dessert named tofu only for its shape) and Jade Parcels (ham and lotus seeds wrapped in vegetable leaves with a spicy broth). Tea is very popular: Qiaoying Village, in the north-west bordering Fontaine, is known for high-quality leaves that are served as drinks or made into tea cakes, and every tea establishment has its own way of serving. Dim sum is a popular breakfast; served with tea it is yum cha.

Farming in rocky Liyue is limited, so crops are concentrated where terraces allow: Qingce Village grows terraced rice that goes to Liyue Harbor to be sold, and sunsettia trees grow across the land. Liyue exports specialties such as Chilibrew and silk; Dawn Winery sells its drinks to Liyue trading unions and merchants who resell them abroad, and Qiaoying's tea supplies local and foreign markets alike. Trade also brings foreign ideas: Xiangling's map notes mention Mondstadt's valberries and a Mondstadt restaurant's matsutake dish, and Xi'er says Xiangling sources some ingredients from Mondstadt.

Wanmin Restaurant (Wanmin-tang) is a deliberate outsider. Chef Mao says Li and Yue are all "Zhongyuan Chop Suey" to him: his kitchen cares about delicious food from everyday ingredients, universally loved flavours and excellent cooking, not systems and frameworks, and he calls those who impose them overcompensating amateurs. Its signature dish is Black-Back Perch Stew, fish cooked with chili oil made from Jueyun Chili and Violetgrass (powdered Violetgrass in the heated oil, per the item text). Xiangling's character story says the dish combines Li richness and strong colour with Yue freshness and nutrition; the Violetgrass touch is the restaurant's secret, which Zhongli mentions in the Stone Harbor Treasure Journal event (limited), with Chef Mao looking baffled in the background. The restaurant sells simple food, ingredients and cooking recipes.

Xiangling's story is the sharpest expression of Liyue's kitchen politics. She learned cooking from her father, who gave her his handwritten journal bearing the line that the most important secret of cooking is passion. At the time the Li-Yue conflict was white-hot and many restaurants, Wanmin included, felt the pressure; she was angered by the monopoly on luxury ingredients like matsutake and crab, and took over the kitchen to make super-delicious dishes out of any ingredient. Her methods are unorthodox: she has used slimes and lizards in recipes, took the hilichurls' clubs for Hilichurl Club BBQ Fish, and wrecks woks in the process. Her Cold-Dressed Fowl left her father on plain congee for two days, since mint and Qingxin flowers did not agree with him, though she herself never seemed affected. Chef Mao says she is constantly inventing dishes and that he sent her off to explore so the restaurant would not confine her; if anyone revolutionises Liyue cuisine, he says, it will be her. Her cooking won acclaim in both Mondstadt and Liyue.

Customer culture at Wanmin is warm and informal: regulars are recognised by their first words, anyone asking whether Xiangling is cooking that day is plainly a regular, and she offers to cook what is not on the menu. Chef Mao notes a young woman with a strange headdress (Ganyu) who often orders only small vegetarian portions; Shenhe later works there as a server after Ganyu's referral, and a Ningguang voice-over notes she has financed the restaurant. During the Moonlight Merriment event (limited) Chef Mao says Xiangling is that year's Masterful Chefs champion.

Regional variation: Within Liyue the contrast is between styles and districts rather than provinces: Li (mountain, rich) versus Yue (sea, light), the polished restaurants of Feiyun Slope versus the street-food leaning Chihu Rock, and the tea villages of the north-west. Qingce Village is rice country; Liyue Harbor draws in every nation's trade.

Compared with Mondstadt, Xi'er likes the fresh, quality produce there but finds Liyue better on seasoning and presentation, and misses spicy food. In an event conversation (Silverwing in Pursuit of the Moon, limited), her older sister Da Xi'er remarks that Snezhnaya's food is made to keep people energetic in the cold and might taste heavy in Liyue, and that Liyue dishes taken north unchanged might seem light there, since environment affects taste. See also Mondstadt and Fontaine cuisine.

Scene use: Use Liyue food for lively, opinionated scenes: a quarrel between a Li-style and a Yue-style loyalist, a crowded Wanmin table with Xiangling at the stove, Xi'er sniffing out a dish's origin, a tea tasting, or a business dinner at an expensive, fully booked restaurant. Characters should talk about ingredients, spice and technique; do not invent prices, menus or recipes beyond the item text.

Contrast settings: diners at the Feiyun Slope houses Liuli Pavilion and Xinyue Kiosk, working people at Chihu Rock, villagers in tea or rice country. Wanmin staff are friendly and informal, so avoid portraying Xiangling as a partisan of Li or Yue; her principle is that good food is good food. Xiangling's experiments with slimes and lizards are known in her circle but not something every diner assumes.

Examples: Black-Back Perch Stew: Wanmin's signature, fish fillets in heated oil with Jueyun Chili and powdered Violetgrass. Jueyun Guoba: crisp rice-and-horsetail crust with ham and Jueyun Chili. Zhongyuan Chop Suey: hearty comfort dish. Almond Tofu: silky chilled almond dessert. Jade Parcels: ham and lotus seeds in vegetable wrappers with a spicy broth. Xinyue Kiosk menu: Crystal Shrimp, Golden Crab, Fullmoon Egg. Tea and tea cakes from Qiaoying Village; dim sum with tea (yum cha) at breakfast.

Status as of 7.1: As of 7.1, Liyue cuisine remains a well-established tradition. Li and Yue still compete, with Liuli Pavilion and Xinyue Kiosk the leading houses, while Wanmin Restaurant has made its mark through Xiangling's innovations, recognised in the Masterful Chefs contest of the Moonlight Merriment event (limited).

25.content: The leading Li-style (mountain delicacy) restaurant in Liyue Harbor, on Feiyun Slope. In the Archon Quest An Organization Known as Wangsheng, Childe arranges a dinner here to introduce the Traveler to Zhongli. Its name (Liuli) can mean glaze, glass or lapis lazuli. A reservation is needed well in advance.

26.content: Renowned as the most authentic Yue-style (seafood-led) restaurant in Liyue, on Feiyun Slope. It is expensive with a long waitlist (about three months per the wiki; about half a year per Xi'er). Its dishes mentioned include Crystal Shrimp, Golden Crab and Fullmoon Egg. During the quest Know Thyself, Know Thy Enemy, the gentry member Maocai meets a Fatui Pyro Agent there.

27.content: A famous restaurant in Chihu Rock, run by Chef Mao, whose daughter Xiangling is head chef. Its map description says some believe its goal is to keep everyone fed, others that it hopes to unify the world's regional cuisines. It sells simple food, ingredients and cooking recipes. Shenhe works there as a server and Ningguang has financed it. Its signature is Black-Back Perch Stew (a dish Xiangling's story credits her with creating).

28.content: A professional gourmet from Chihu Rock met in Mondstadt, who came to taste its food after hearing Xiangling sources ingredients there. She explains Li and Yue styles to the Traveler, calls herself fair and impartial despite being a Liyue native, and misses spicy food. Her older sister is Da Xi'er.

29.content: A village in north-west Liyue bordering Fontaine, known for producing high-quality tea; its leaves are served as drinks or made into tea cakes and supply local and foreign markets. Serving tea is complex and each establishment has its own approach.

30.content:
Daily Life in Liyue (also: Liyue daily life, everyday life in Liyue, Liyue customs): Everyday life in Liyue, the Geo nation of contracts, runs on trade. Liyue Harbor is the busiest commercial hub in Teyvat, with merchants from every nation, and the villages around it are mostly home to the young and the old while able-bodied people go to the city for work. People drink tea, argue over cooking styles, trust written agreements, revere the adepti of the mountains, and are governed by the Liyue Qixing, a council of merchants, rather than by a god.

Liyue's mood is practical and orderly: bargains are honoured, goods and gossip travel fast, and traditions (festivals, idioms, habits around tea and furniture) are taken seriously without being stiff. The people now live under mortal governance, with the adepti guarding the land and stepping in only if humans cannot cope. Most residents do not follow high politics; life in the Harbor goes on as normal even on days of great ceremony.

Rocky, mountainous terrain makes farming harder than in Mondstadt, so Liyue leans on mining, smithing, crafts, tea and sea trade. The country is also marked by its past: farmland on the Guili Plains ruined in the Archon War, ancient devices such as the Guizhong Ballista and Dunyu Ruins, and the slow reopening of the Chasm mines.

Practice: Common routines: haggling and contract-making, tea and dim sum, visits to restaurants and teahouses, hiring escorts for goods, pilgrimages toward the adepti, festivals such as the Lantern Rite and Moonchase, and sending children to tutors or martial clans.

Settlement: many people live in villages such as Mingyun, Qingce and Qiaoying, but Liyue Harbor is the great centre. Villages that cannot support their people are abandoned; Mingyun Village emptied when its ore ran out and its people moved west for better prospects, and other abandoned settlements dot the nation.

Farming and goods: Qingce Village keeps terraced rice fields whose harvest is sold in the Harbor, sunsettia trees grow across the country, and Qiaoying Village is known for tea leaves served as drinks or made into tea cakes. Every establishment serves tea its own way, and tea bags would seem foreign.

Food: breakfast often includes dim sum, taken with tea as yum cha. Liyue has two rival culinary styles, the bold, rich Li style from mountain ingredients and the lighter Yue style that favours seafood. Their fans bicker constantly; in the Harbor's Feiyun Slope shopping district, Liuli Pavilion is the well-regarded Li-style restaurant and Xinyue Kiosk the Yue-style one. Chihu Rock, the poorer end of the city, favours street food, with newer places such as Wanmin Restaurant.

Trade: Liyue Harbor handles commerce with Mondstadt, Inazuma, Sumeru and likely Snezhnaya, while Yilong Wharf mainly handles trade with Fontaine. Liyue is known abroad for cloth and silk (cloth goes to Inazuma), tea and Chilibrew, and local merchants resell Dawn Winery drinks. Roads still need protection, so many merchants hire local security agencies; being independently run, these are hard for the Qixing to standardise, and the Sword and Strongbox Secure Transport Agency is among the better known.

Language: people use idioms constantly (for example "the walls have ears," "money belongs to the world outside your head," "food is life"), and a local script resembling seal script appears on signs.

Education and clans: schooling appears to depend on family means. Wealthy households hire tutors (Xingqiu is well educated), while people of lower standing may be illiterate, as the Adventurers' Guild's Lan says of herself. Some people instead join clans to learn martial arts, such as the Guhua Clan, whose arts are Raincutter for swords, Light Piercer for polearms and Life Ender for mastery of both. Swords and polearms are the typical weapons of Liyue, and Morax is praised there as the Warrior God.

Medicine: Liyue's medicine is relatively comprehensive. Baizhu is a renowned physician and Bubu Pharmacy is known beyond Liyue, though few know he draws on Changsheng's powers. Herbs such as violetgrass are common ingredients, and Chenyu Vale keeps its own medical practices.

Home and architecture: buildings follow ancient-Chinese-inspired styles with eaved roofs and warm colours. In a study, furnishings must be placed at set positions and angles; Zhongli says there are three schools of thought and nine specialisations on this.

Industry: mining and smithing are important. Blackcliff Forge produced the Blackcliff and Prototype weapon series and doubles as a mine. The Chasm is the nation's best-known mine and employs many miners; the Qixing closed it after incidents and later let small groups of experienced miners return. The Eight Trades, eight commerce sectors under the Qixing, oversee industries.

Religion and the adepti: many people revere the adepti and some make pilgrimages to their abodes in Jueyun Karst. The Wangsheng Funeral Parlor, run by the Hu family, handles funerals.

Government in daily life: the Qixing run the nation from Yuehai Pavilion. The wiki's culture page has Ningguang (Tianquan) handling law, Keqing (Yuheng) land, building and employment, and Uncle Tian (Tianshu) policy. The Millelith double as peacekeepers, keep outposts along common roads against monsters and bandits, and are heavily present in the Harbor. Treasure Hoarders are more active in Liyue than elsewhere and prowl lonely roads and the Chasm. The Yuheng's work against banditry has made roads safer, but demand for escorts remains high.

The Rite of Descension: each year the Qixing invited Rex Lapis to give predictions for the coming year, which shaped policy and business. It was open to everyone and drew visitors, including Liyue natives living abroad, though most Harbor residents carried on as usual. A Rite of Parting, by contrast, commemorates a deceased adeptus.

Motifs: Liyue design uses geometric patterns such as meanders and diamonds, auspicious clouds, wan, thunder, ruyi and shou symbols, and scales as an emblem.

Music: Liyue's music favours classical string and wind instruments such as the erhu, guzheng and dizi.

Regional variation: Harbor versus village. The Harbor is cosmopolitan, loud and rich, with quarters from the wealthy Feiyun Slope to humbler Chihu Rock. Villages are quieter, older in population, and tied to one crop or craft: rice at Qingce, tea at Qiaoying, formerly ore at Mingyun.

Mountain and sea. Jueyun Karst is the home of adepti and hermits and a pilgrimage destination; Yilong Wharf is the trade gate toward Fontaine, with a small, discreet Millelith unit; the Chasm region is miners' country; and Chenyu Vale has its own healing customs.

Scene use: Good hooks: a merchant haggling and insisting on a written contract; a heated debate over Li versus Yue cooking; tea served in a way that matters to the host; a stranger hiring a security agency for a risky delivery; a villager moving to the city for work; a pilgrim heading toward the mountains; idioms used as polite warnings. Keep the tone businesslike, hospitable and rooted in reputation.

For depth, contrast wealthy and poor, remind characters that the Qixing govern and the adepti watch, and let ancient history (Guili Plains, the Chasm) surface in ruins or stories without resolving mysteries canon leaves open.

31.comment: Daily Life in Liyue: Li and Yue Culinary Styles
31.content: Liyue has two long-standing culinary styles: Li, bold and rich, built on mountain ingredients, and Yue, lighter and built on seafood. Fans of each are in a perpetual feud. In the Harbor's Feiyun Slope district, Liuli Pavilion is the notable Li-style restaurant and Xinyue Kiosk the Yue-style one.

32.comment: Daily Life in Liyue: Tea in Liyue
32.content: Tea is very popular in Liyue. Qiaoying Village is famed for its leaves, which can be served as drinks or turned into tea cakes. Each establishment serves tea in its own way, and tea bags are an unfamiliar idea. Dim sum is a common breakfast, called yum cha when taken with tea.

33.comment: Daily Life in Liyue: Moonchase Festival Origins
33.content: A festival of reunion and feasting, organised by the Qixing, who choose a theme each year. It honours Marchosius, the Stove God who taught the people of the Guili Assembly to make fire and cook. Rex Lapis later unified older human festivals, including what Keqing's grandfather called the Stove God Festival, under the Moonchase name.

34.comment: Daily Life in Liyue: Guhua Clan Martial Arts
34.content: A Liyue martial lineage whose three arts are Raincutter (swords), Light Piercer (polearms) and Life Ender (both). The brotherhood that preceded the clan was founded by an associate of Guhua, who himself wielded the claymore Rainslasher. Xingqiu practises Guhua sword style. Joining a clan is one path to training besides formal schooling.

35.comment: Daily Life in Liyue: Liyue Idioms
35.content: Liyue is known for idioms and sayings used in everyday talk, such as "the walls have ears" (be careful what you say), "the hunter by day is the hunted by night" (roles reverse), "don't always call it as you see it" (be tactful), "food is life," "money belongs to the world outside your head" and "we will meet again." In English localisation some are reworded to keep the spirit.

36.content:
Liyue Fashion (also: Liyue clothing, Liyue attire, Liyue dress, clothing of Liyue): Liyue dress draws on Chinese clothing traditions such as the hanfu, qipao and tangzhuang, without following any single historical dynasty. Ordinary people wear vests, shirts and long or knee-length dresses; some groups wear recognisable uniforms, among them the Millelith, restaurant waitstaff, the Wangsheng Funeral Parlor and exorcists.

Canon never names Liyue's styles; the comparisons to real-world dress come from how the game's NPC designs look. In the sources read, clothing mainly signals age, trade and affiliation rather than a formal dress code.

Practice: Boys and men wear shirts and vests; girls wear short dresses, and women in Liyue Harbor wear long dresses with qipao-like details. Elderly characters have their own cuts. Several jobs have uniforms.

Men's dress appears in variants for boys, adult men and older men. Some shirts are based on the tangzhuang, visible in the decoration across the chest. Suling is a customised variant: he wears the vest without a shirt beneath and binds his torso with bandages. Girls tend to wear short, knee-length dresses resembling the qipao. Women who live in Liyue Harbor wear long dresses with similar details. Madame Ping's clothes seem to be inspired by the hanfu, which the wiki reads as a nod to her great age.

Uniforms mark jobs. The Millelith have separate soldier and officer uniforms; waitstaff at Liyue restaurants appear in matching outfits in brown or red; and the Wangsheng Funeral Parlor has male and female uniforms worn by undertakers such as Ferrylady and Meng. Exorcists and thaumaturges have recognisable attire of their own. Chongyun's default outfit, Pure Spirit, is described in game as a traditional thaumaturge's trappings: a symmetrical white hooded jacket with navy embroidery over a blue shirt and white pants with gold cuffs, with bandages at his right wrist and ankle. Shenhe, from the same clan, is shown in a variation of the same style. No ordinary NPC wears exorcist attire.

Equipment and clothing connect to Liyue Harbor's trades. The Millelith's equipment is supplied by the Blackcliff Forge, and Turenna said they were developing armor of ceramic blocks wedged between pieces of hardened fabric (see the limited-time entry below). Fabric work is one of the trade sectors that Liyue Harbor's character-card emblems represent, through the Silk Flower, which stands for fabric trades such as the Feiyun Commerce Guild as well as herbal and pharmaceutical trades such as Bubu Pharmacy.

Regional variation: The wiki's Fashion section covers Liyue Harbor and nearby NPCs. Harbor women are the group specifically said to wear long qipao-style dresses; the sources do not describe separate dress for the villages, the mountains or the adepti's abodes beyond individual characters.

Characters show individual variation rather than regional uniforms: Xinyan's sleeves carry a triple-diamond pattern, and the back of Zhongli's coat carries a Geo Archon motif of a central diamond with smaller diamonds at the corners, the same symbol found at Yuehai Pavilion. Whether these patterns have an in-world meaning on clothing is not stated.

Motifs: Liyue design favours geometric decoration. Meanders and diamonds recur across emblems, and a stylised cloud pattern (xiangyun, "auspicious clouds") is a traditional motif. The multi-diamond shapes are likely based on a traditional Chinese motif (fangsheng), per the wiki. Zhongli's coat and Xinyan's sleeves are the clothing examples.

The character-card frames use Liyue emblems that are interface art rather than clothing: adepti-related characters (Ganyu, Qiqi, Xianyun, Xiao, Yanfei, Zhongli and Zibai) carry a dragon, stag, qilin and crane, while other Liyue characters carry trade emblems (Mora, Silk Flower, ship, crossed sword and polearm). They are noted only because they show how the game groups Liyue's trades.

Scene use: Use clothing to place a character quickly: a vest and rolled sleeves for a laborer, a long qipao-style dress for a Harbor woman, a hooded white jacket for an exorcist, a plain uniform for an undertaker at night. Avoid naming real-world dynasties in character dialogue.

Add small, concrete details: bandages on a wrist, a Vision worn on a belt, embroidered trim. Remember the custom Ferrylady describes: in Liyue it is generally not customary to speak to Wangsheng staff, who work silently around mourners at night, so a character in that uniform may be formal and reserved by habit.

Do not claim fixed rank colours or insignia for the Millelith, and do not invent specific tailors, fabrics or guilds beyond those named in canon.

Examples: Chongyun's Pure Spirit outfit (exorcist attire); Ferrylady and Meng (Wangsheng Funeral Parlor uniforms); Hongyu and Zhenhai (Millelith soldier and officer uniforms, shown as images on the wiki); Madame Ping (hanfu-inspired elderly dress); Suling (bandaged variation of the vest).

37.comment: Liyue Fashion: Character Outfits of Liyue
37.content:
Game cosmetics rather than in-world clothing, but they show how Liyue designs are imagined. Chongyun's default Pure Spirit is described as a traditional thaumaturge's trappings. Ningguang's Orchid's Evening Gown is formal wear with a long cyan skirt and butterfly ornaments at the ankles. Keqing's Opulent Splendor is described as formal wear woven from Silk Flower petals and violetgrass dye, fusing Liyue and exotic styles. Ganyu's Twilight Blossom (4.4) is a festive outfit in nightshade black and cerulean blue with Qingxin-inspired ornaments.

Orchid's Evening Gown was a free reward during the Fleeting Colors in Flight event in version 2.4 (limited then) and has been sold in the outfit shop since 2.5. Treat these as optional cosmetics in roleplay, not default dress.

38.comment: Liyue Fashion: Wangsheng Funeral Parlor Uniform
38.content: Undertakers of the Wangsheng Funeral Parlor, such as Ferrylady and Meng, wear a recognisable parlor uniform (the wiki shows male and female versions). The parlor is run by the Hu family and has served Liyue Harbor for generations. Ferrylady says it is generally not customary in Liyue to speak to its staff. See the faction entry for the parlor itself.

39.content: The Millelith have standard soldier and officer uniforms (wiki examples: Hongyu and Zhenhai). Their standard weapon is the White Tassel, and Blackcliff Forge supplies their equipment. Their uniform colours and insignia are not described in the sources read.

40.content: During the limited-time Mutual Security Enhancing Simulation event (the quest Commanders and Wargames), Turenna said the Millelith were developing armor of ceramic blocks wedged between pieces of hardened fabric, meant to spread the impact of projectiles. Whether it has been issued is not stated.

41.content:
Liyue Opera (also: opera of Liyue, Liyue Harbor opera): Liyue Opera is a traditional art of Liyue: plays told through singing, acting, dance and spoken parts, performed by troupes, with sophisticated vocals and richly varied melodies. The best-known troupe is the Yun-Han Opera Troupe of Liyue Harbor, run by the playwright and singer Yun Jin, who performs from time to time at Heyu Tea House. Many traditional plays dramatise the adepti and Rex Lapis, such as "The Divine Damsel of Devastation".

Canon calls it one of Liyue's traditional arts, passed down for generations and much changed from its original form while keeping its refined vocals and varied melodies. Performers normally work in troupes. It is a living, popular entertainment in Liyue Harbor: fans ask at Heyu Tea House about performance schedules, wealthy patrons such as Ningguang donate to troupes, and outlanders such as Kaedehara Kazuha come to listen.

Practice: Performers sing, act and dance, and training is long and physical. Full tradition calls for wrapped hair, full-face makeup and an elaborate costume. A troupe is led by a director, who may also be its lead performer and playwright.

Training begins in childhood and is harsh: stretching exercises, memorising lyrics, and whole days of dance practice in the sun. Yun Jin learned from her mother, a former star of Liyue Harbor, whom she calls a very strict teacher, and her father is a playwright. Daily voice rehearsal is a core habit: she says that if you skip a day only you know, but skip three and the audience knows. Stage combat is part of the work, which is why she took up the polearm. A troupe keeps veteran members, a manager, and wardrobe and props staff, while the director makes the major decisions.

Costume and makeup are demanding. Yun Jin remarks that full dress is spectacular but exhausting, so she performs without full makeup or hair-wrapping whenever she has the option. She describes opera customs as very particular and handed down through generations, so performers sometimes know how a convention is done without knowing why; she is delighted that Zhongli knows the origins of almost everything. A well-regarded performer can fill a house: Fan Er'ye, boss of Heyu Tea House, says one Yun Jin performance earns enough Mora that the house need not open for a month.

Repertoire and taste are in tension. Yun Jin's profile says adeptal and Rex Lapis stories make up the majority of the traditional repertoire, because people love fantasies about the adepti. Early in her career she grew dissatisfied when pitch and tempo rose or fell the same way in every play and characters began to blur together; she compares the girl in "The Divine Damsel of Devastation" with the fisherman's daughter in "String of Pearls". She credits a monodrama, "Snow Treading", with teaching her to leave herself behind and walk in a character's shoes; her Vision turned up in her sleeve after that performance. She now writes plays about ordinary people's loves, angers and obsessions. Troupe elders, by contrast, are strongly traditional and frown on other music such as rock 'n' roll, so she attends Xinyan's gigs discreetly.

Repertoire: Named plays in canon: "The Divine Damsel of Devastation", a traditional adeptal play the Yun-Han troupe has performed, with a new ending written by Yun Jin; "String of Pearls", written by Yun Jin, in which she plays the lead Zixin; and "Snow Treading", a monodrama about a strenuous walk in the snow. Yun Jin has written all the other new plays the troupe has staged in recent years.

Because Liyue legends centre on gods and adepti, supernatural subjects dominate the repertoire. Yun Jin wishes to sing of human stories instead, and once dreamed of performing in an adeptus's abode, perhaps at Jueyun Karst, so that adepti and people alike could hear her.

Regional variation: In these sources Liyue Opera is a Liyue Harbor art that also travels. The Yun-Han troupe performs at Heyu Tea House and, per a later anecdote, on a stage at Yilong Wharf. During the Lantern Rite event Fleeting Colors in Flight, Granny Ruoxin of Qingce Village invited Yun Jin to perform at the village. Other nations' equivalents are not described in the sources read.

Scene use: Good scene beats: patrons asking at the tea house when Yun Jin will appear; backstage rituals such as cleaning a lucky lock before curtain; traditionalist troupe elders versus a modernising director; Zhongli attending as a connoisseur. Keep Yun Jin polished in public and friendly in private. Do not invent plots for operas beyond the titles and themes canon gives.

Performers treat practice as discipline and even pleasure rather than burden. Audiences reward spectacle but also sincerity.

Examples: Yun Jin performing at Heyu Tea House, and Zhongli watching her at Yilong Wharf, are the main canon examples. In the Zhongli anecdote (Travelers' Tales, added 5.4) he praises her command of the folk art and regrets letting his tea go cold.

42.content:
Liyue Harbor's most famous opera troupe, directed by Yun Jin and currently performing at Heyu Tea House. The Yun family were famous weaponsmiths about five hundred years ago before turning to opera as a family tradition; the troupe was established by the time of Yun Jin's paternal grandfather, and many veterans date from his directorship. Yunning is the manager and Yinggong handles wardrobe and props. The "Han" in the name is unrelated to the Han family of weaponsmiths; the character differs.

Troupe elders fuss over Yun Jin's diet and voice and disapprove of rock 'n' roll. Ningguang has made several generous donations to the troupe, according to Yun Jin.

43.comment: Liyue Opera: The Divine Damsel of Devastation
43.content: A traditional Liyue opera about the adepti, named in Yun Jin's profile as a prime example of the genre. The Yun-Han troupe has performed it recently with a new ending written by Yun Jin. The sources read do not give its plot.

44.comment: Liyue Opera: Heyu Tea House Performances
44.content: Heyu Tea House in Liyue Harbor is owned by Fan Er'ye, a former performer. It draws crowds with a top storyteller, Tea Master Liu Su, and with the Yun-Han troupe. Yun Jin takes the stage from time to time, so fans gather hoping to catch her, and nine in ten patrons are said to be her fans.

45.comment: Liyue Opera: Granny Ruoxin and Fleeting Colors in Flight
45.content: During the Lantern Rite event Fleeting Colors in Flight (2.4), Granny Ruoxin of Qingce Village invited Yun Jin to perform an opera there, and an event idle line has her say Yun Jin always brings something new. Ruoxin herself, in permanent dialogue, was once an actress at Heyu Tea House alongside Fan Er'ye. The invitation is limited-event material.

46.content:
Religion in Liyue (also: Liyue faith, worship of Rex Lapis, Geo Archon worship, adepti reverence): Liyue's faith centres on Rex Lapis (Morax), the Geo Archon and god of contracts and commerce, who guided the nation for over three thousand years, and on the adepti, mountain-dwelling immortals who protect Liyue from afar. Worship is practical and ritual-minded: wishes at censers, offerings at Jueyun Karst, the yearly Rite of Descension, and funeral rites for departing adepti. In Chapter I Rex Lapis stages his death and retires; the Liyue Qixing and the adepti now carry on, and the god lives as the mortal Zhongli.

Liyue folk emphasise that their god has always been with them: unlike Mondstadt's absent Archon, Rex Lapis walked with the city through its history, and locals describe him as a father who handles everything. His authority is the root of Liyue's contract culture and of Mora, the currency named after Morax. Outsiders are expected to say Rex Lapis, not Morax, as the courteous form.

The adepti are revered almost as deities: they are mostly illuminated beasts, and Liyue people make offerings and occasional pilgrimages to Jueyun Karst, the sacred mountain land where mortals do not tread without a Sigil of Permission. After Chapter I the Qixing's public account is that Rex Lapis failed a divine trial and his soul regained the celestial heights, while Madame Ping tells the Qixing that the age of contracts between gods and Liyue has passed and the age of contracts between Liyue and its people has begun. The adepti accept humans governing Liyue, though they will step in if humans cannot protect it.

Belief is layered: formal state ritual run by the Qixing, popular wish-making, folk legends of stone-statue adepti and adepti trials, and an expert tradition of funerary etiquette preserved by the Wangsheng Funeral Parlor, which keeps rites for adepti that are rarely needed.

Practice: Annual state ritual: the Rite of Descension, in which the Qixing invited Rex Lapis to give predictions for the year, was held at Yujing Terrace until Chapter I. At the rite people prayed and wished at censers, believing adepti and the god blessed the day. Nationwide, the Lantern Rite and Moonchase Festival are Liyue's great festivals. Pilgrims leave offerings at the edge of Jueyun Karst. When an adeptus departs, the Rite of Parting is held.

Liyue's Statues of the Seven carry Geo: the Liyue statues look different from Mondstadt's, and legend says the monumental Geo Archon statue that watches over Liyue was sculpted in the god's image. Rex Lapis's role as guarantor of Mora and of contracts gives commercial acts a religious weight (see culture.liyue-contracts). Exorcists and thaumaturges, such as Chongyun's clan, form a related spiritual tradition.

Some adepti use sacred names (the Chinese text gives Rex Lapis a higher-ranking sacred name than most adepti, and Prime of Adepti is another of his titles; Madame Ping has a sacred name, Streetward Rambler, but goes by her alias, and it is unclear whether Ganyu has one), and the Wangsheng Funeral Parlor's Zhongli oversees rituals down to costume, timing, place and audience. Legends hold that some adepti asked Morax to turn them into stone statues and that the statues move, a story recorded in the Records of Jueyun.

Regional variation: Liyue Harbor holds the state rituals; villages like Qingce and Mingyun are home to older and younger residents and keep quieter local customs. Jueyun Karst, in the northwest of Liyue, is the adepti's land. No organised church is shown; mortals manage public life.

Chenyu Vale and its adepti (Lingyuan, the Herblord, Fujin) have their own history from the Archon War, when the vale's unnamed mistress fought Morax and, at the end, her own adepti rebelled against her to save the valley from her flood; locals there also keep their own medicine and traditions.

Scene use: Use incense, wishes, bells, and a keen sense of propriety. Locals speak of Rex Lapis in the respectful third person and still pray to him. After Chapter I, ordinary people believe the official story that his soul returned to the heavens; only a few know he lives as Zhongli. Adepti speak of mortals with affection but expect certain etiquette. A foreigner who says "Morax" in front of a Liyue native may be corrected.

Characters differ: Madame Ping, Cloud Retainer and Zhongli view the gods' era with weary affection; Ningguang and Keqing speak in the Qixing's practical, contract-minded voice; Hu Tao treats death with irreverent ease while respecting ritual form.

Examples: - Chapter I: the Rite of Descension ends in a staged death, and the Rite of Parting later marks the god's retirement.
- Childe tells the Traveler that Liyue people believe Jueyun Karst is the adepti's home and leave offerings at its borders, while he knows they really exist.

47.comment: Religion in Liyue: Rex Lapis as a deity
47.content: Rex Lapis is the Geo Archon, oldest of the Seven, called the God of Contracts, Commerce and War, the Prime of Adepti, the Lord of Geo and (outside Liyue) Morax. Mora is named for him. He led Liyue through the Archon War, resettled his people south of Mt. Tianheng after Guizhong's death and made a contract with the adepti to guard the harbor. In the main story he feigns death at the Rite of Descension, passes his Gnosis to the Tsaritsa's emissary Signora and retires; his character entry carries the detail.

48.comment: Religion in Liyue: The adepti and Jueyun Karst
48.content: Most adepti retired into seclusion at Jueyun Karst after the Archon War. Mortals who enter without a Sigil of Permission risk offending them, and Liyue people leave offerings at the borders. Some adepti remain in the harbor, Ganyu as the Qixing's secretary and Madame Ping at Yujing Terrace, while Xiao hunts demons as the last yaksha. When Rex Lapis stepped down, the adepti agreed to let humans govern but remain ready to defend Liyue.

49.comment: Religion in Liyue: Descension and Parting
49.content: Two paired state rites. The Rite of Descension was the yearly invitation to Rex Lapis; the Rite of Parting is the funeral for a departed adeptus or god, held for him in Chapter I. Both are described in their own entries.

50.content:
Liyue Script (also: Liyue language, Liyue writing, Liyue characters, Liyue seal script, Liyue local language): The Liyue Script is the angular, character-based writing seen on shop signs, banners, notice boards and scrolls in Liyue, especially around Liyue Harbor. "Liyue Script" is an unofficial name. Its look is modelled on real Chinese seal script. It is background texture for a scene, not a code that characters are shown deciphering.

The same lettering shows up in a few other places: the Jade Chamber intel wall in an animated cutscene, a poetry gala banner, some character skill effects, and the seal in the domain Beneath the Dragon-Queller.

Practice: Merchants and notice boards in Liyue carry it. Visually it is blocky and square, built from strokes rather than an alphabet. Canon never has a character explain how it is read.

In Liyue Harbor, shop signs repeat the same small set of glyphs: stalls, a bank, a teahouse, an antique shop, a jeweller, the dockyard and a pharmacy share the same eight symbols, with only a few exceptions (the last symbol on one restaurant banner and the bookstore signs). In scene terms, the writing reads as a familiar visual style rather than as distinct, readable shop names.

Skill effects use the same glyphs. Characters of the script ring around Chongyun while his blade infusion is active and appear when Zhongli's stone stele breaks. Yanfei's charged attack leaves a stamp-like mark of four characters, which the community reads as blessing, prosperity, business and seal. This fits her work as a legal adviser, but the readings are fan interpretation, not canon text.

The Serenitea Pot's Adeptal Mirror and the Neighboring Nations Congenial Poetry Gala banner (Waterborne Poetry event) also carry it. Because the glyphs repeat so much, treat any invented translation of a sign as flavour you made up for the scene, not as a canon reading.

Regional variation: Inside Liyue the script is a civic and commercial presence, strongest in Liyue Harbor. No canon source describes how it differs between Liyue towns, and other nations have their own scripts.

A stylised or ancient-looking form appears on the ground around the seal after Azhdaha is defeated in Beneath the Dragon-Queller. Four glyphs at the seal's centre mark which element Azhdaha will be infused with, and are based on seal-script forms for Electro, Hydro, Cryo and Pyro; the Electro glyph is simplified by swapping part of it for the game's Electro symbol. Whether this ancient form is an official separate script is not stated in canon.

Deciphered characters: Community decipherment finds that some glyphs closely match real seal script, but they often do not form clean sentences.
